patch.value: history-compact renumbers version identifiers, so pm get --at N and pm restore N address a different recorded state after compaction with exit 0 and no signal

Version numbers are the only addressing scheme pm offers for the immutable record besides timestamps, and history-compact silently rebases them. Before compaction pm get <id> --at 3 returned the state recorded at entry 3. After 'pm history-compact <id> --before 6' the same command returns the state recorded at the original entry 7, exits 0, and emits no warning, no deprecation, and no mapping. Timestamp addressing behaves correctly across the same boundary (a pruned timestamp is refused with history_target_out_of_range exit 2), so the two addressing schemes diverge: one is stable under compaction and the other silently changes meaning. Every stored reference to a version number - in a comment, a close reason, an external audit record, a script, a downstream tracker - becomes a reference to different content at the moment a stream is compacted, and nothing in the record says so. The synthetic baseline entry records only the free-text message 'history-compact baseline snapshot before 6.' and carries no structured field for the compacted-entry count or the version offset, so no consumer can mechanically translate a pre-compaction version to its post-compaction equivalent or determine that a given version number predates the boundary. The baseline entry is also stamped with the compaction wall-clock time while occupying index 1, so after compaction the stream's index order and timestamp order disagree: index 1 ts 14:55:39 precedes index 2 ts 14:54:53. pm history --verify --strict-exit exits 0 throughout, so no integrity check observes any of this.

A version identifier resolves to the same recorded state before and after compaction, or the pre-boundary identifier is refused with a distinct machine-readable code rather than silently resolving to different content; The compaction baseline entry records the compacted-entry count and the version offset as structured fields, so a reader can mechanically map a pre-compaction version number to its post-compaction equivalent or classify it as pruned; A read or restore targeting a version that predates the compaction boundary is reported as intentionally unavailable, distinguishable by code from an out-of-range target that never existed; The stream's index order and timestamp order agree after compaction, or the baseline entry's timestamp semantics are declared in the format specification and asserted by a test; history --verify fails, or a dedicated check fails, on a stream whose version addressing changed meaning without a recorded offset - proven by a negative-control fixture; The evidence in this item's description is reproduced as a regression test that compacts a stream and asserts version-identifier stability or refusal
Make version addressing stable under compaction, or make its instability explicit, recorded, and refusable
Restoring an item to any version at any time is the core durability promise; an identifier that silently changes meaning turns a correct-looking restore into undetected data substitution
Silent wrong answer on point-in-time reads and restores after any compaction

The mandate is that any item can be restored to any version at any time and that the record is immutable proof; compaction is the one shipped operation that breaks the identifier the promise is written in, and it passes every existing integrity check
pm create Task V1; for i in 2..10 pm update <id> --title V$i; pm get <id> --at 3 -> V3; pm history-compact <id> --before 6; pm get <id> --at 3 -> V7 (exit 0)
pm get <id> --at 3 returns the same recorded state before and after compaction, or refuses with a pruned-version code
Before compaction --at 3 returns the state titled V3; after compacting before v6 the same command returns the state titled V7 with exit 0 and no warning

value.text:
Reproduced live 2026-08-07 in an isolated sandbox, and the reproduction shows the two addressing schemes have opposite safety properties on the same verb.

Nine history entries were built on one item, each update setting a distinguishable description. Before compaction, `pm restore <id> 3` exits 0 and yields description "version 2", which is the state entry 3 recorded. `pm history-compact <id> --before 6` then reports entries_compacted 5, entries_retained 5, first_retained_entry 6, and rewrites the stream as a synthetic baseline plus the retained tail, renumbered densely from 1. The identical call `pm restore <id> 3` now exits 0 and yields "version 6". Same command, same item, same repository, different reconstructed state, no warning and no offset in the envelope.

Two additional facts that sharpen the AC set rather than widening it. First, `pm restore <id> 1` succeeds and yields "version 4": version 1 is now the history_compact_baseline, whose replay reconstructs the state at the compaction boundary, so the earliest addressable version is not the earliest recorded version and nothing says so. Second, the timestamp scheme is correct where the version scheme is not: a pre-boundary ISO timestamp is refused with history_target_out_of_range at exit 2, and an out-of-range high version number (99) is also refused with the same code. So the refusal machinery already exists and is reached from both ends of the range; it cannot fire in the middle because after compaction the numbering is dense from 1 again and a pruned version is indistinguishable from a present one.

Throughout all of it `pm history <id> --verify --strict-exit` exits 0. The record is provably intact and provably mis-addressed at the same time, which is the state AC3 exists to make impossible. The point-in-time read has the same defect as the mutation: `pm get <id> --at 3` returns the post-compaction state with no signal. The mutation is the worse half, because a restore appends a hash-anchored entry whose recorded intent no longer denotes what it denoted when it was written.
